======================================================================
COMPLETE EMPIRICAL RESEARCH PLAN
======================================================================

1. IDENTIFICATION STRATEGY
----------------------------------------------------------------------
I use a two–stage least-squares (2SLS) instrumental-variables design in
which Difference-in-Differences (DID) variation generated by two exogenous
regulatory shocks—(i) the Insider Trading Sanctions Act (ITSA, Oct-1984)
and (ii) the Insider Trading and Securities Fraud Enforcement Act
(ITSFEA, Nov-1988)—serves as the instrument for pre-bid runups.

Rationale
•  The central causal parameter is β in  Markupᵢ = α + β·Runupᵢ + Xᵢγ + εᵢ.  
   Because Runupᵢ is endogenous (it reflects private information about
   deal synergies, leak propensity, etc.), OLS is biased.  
•  ITSA and ITSFEA sharply raised statutory penalties and SEC resources
   for insider trading, reducing the expected net benefit of trading on
   leaked information and therefore the size and frequency of pre-bid
   runups.  The laws were economy-wide, externally imposed and unrelated
   to any individual pending deal, providing powerful quasi-experimental
   variation.  
•  Their impact is heterogeneous: industries historically associated with
   more insider-trading prosecutions (“High-Leak” industries) experienced
   much larger drops in abnormal volume than did “Low-Leak” industries.
   Interacting the time shocks with this cross-sectional exposure gives a
   strong, deal-level instrument.

First stage (DID):
Runupᵢ = π₀ + π₁·PostLawₜ + π₂·HighLeakⱼ + π₃·PostLawₜ×HighLeakⱼ + Xᵢδ + uᵢ  

Second stage:
Markupᵢ = α + β·Ŕunupᵢ (predicted) + Xᵢγ + εᵢ

If β = –1  → complete substitution  
If β = 0   → complete addition  
Intermediate values signal partial substitution.

2. TREATMENT AND CONTROL
----------------------------------------------------------------------
Treatment variable (endogenous)  
   Runupᵢ  = cumulative market-adjusted return of the target over trading
             days [–42, –1] relative to the first bid announcement.

Instrument (DID “treatment”)
   Zᵢ  = PostLawₜ × HighLeakⱼ, where  
     PostLawₜ  = 1 for deals whose announcement date falls:  
                 • Oct-1984 – Oct-1988 (ITSA window) or  
                 • Nov-1988 – Dec-1991 (ITSFEA window)  
                 with separate indicators for each statute in robustness.  
     HighLeakⱼ = 1 if the target’s 2-digit SIC is in the top quartile of
                 insider-trading prosecutions per 100 listed firms over
                 1978-1983 (pre-law baseline), 0 otherwise.

Control group  
   Observations with (PostLaw = 0) or (HighLeak = 0) act as controls in
   the DID; the IV is therefore constructed from differential exposure.

Treatment timing / event date  
   The announcement date (day 0) is fixed by Comment’s database.  All
   variables are relative to that date.  To avoid anticipation/lag
   issues, a six-month “wash-out” window (Mar-1984–Sep-1984 and May-1988–Oct-1988)
   is omitted from the main analysis.

3. KEY IDENTIFYING ASSUMPTIONS
----------------------------------------------------------------------
A1. Relevance (First-stage)  
    ITSA/ITSFEA × HighLeak significantly reduce Runup.  Plausible given
    contemporaneous evidence on volume and return declines after both
    statutes; testable (F-stat > 10).  

A2. Exogeneity (Exclusion)  
    Conditional on controls and fixed effects, the statutes affect the
    post-announcement markup only through their effect on Runup, not
    through other deal-value channels.  Plausible: laws regulate trading
    in target shares but do **not** change antitrust law, tax law, or
    takeover mechanisms.  

A3. Parallel trends (DID component)  
    In the absence of the law, Runups in High- versus Low-Leak industries
    would have followed parallel trends.  Testable in pre-period placebo
    windows (1975-1983) and visually in event-time plots.  

A4. No simultaneity / SUTVA  
    Each deal’s runup and markup are unaffected by the treatment status
    of other deals; reasonable because deals are idiosyncratic.  

A5. Monotonicity  
    The statutes do not increase runups for any target (no “defiers”).
    Reasonable given uniformly higher penalties.

4. THREATS TO IDENTIFICATION & MITIGATION
----------------------------------------------------------------------
T1. Concurrent Takeover-market Shocks  
    • Drexel junk-bond collapse (1989) or poison-pill diffusion may alter
      markups directly.  
    Mitigation: include year×industry fixed effects and explicit controls
      for junk-bond market index spreads, poison-pill adoption, and
      hostile-bid indicator.

T2. Sample-selection Bias (only successful deals)  
    If higher runups also change the probability of deal completion, the
    observed sample is selected.  
    Mitigation: re-estimate in full 1,398 deals (incl. later than 1-year)
      and in universe of announced deals from SDC (placebo).  Use
      Heckman selectivity correction with a first-stage probit on
      completion.

T3. Measurement Error in Runup  
    Bid rumors may lead to unclear “announcement” dates, attenuating
    β.  
    Mitigation: use alternative announcement dates from Factiva and
      re-define runup windows (–63, –1), (–30, –1).  IV also alleviates
      classical measurement error.

5. R CODE OUTLINE
----------------------------------------------------------------------
```r
# -------------------------------------------
# 0. Packages
# -------------------------------------------
library(data.table)   # fast data ops
library(fixest)       # IV and FE regressions
library(lmtest)       # Wald tests
library(sandwich)     # robust vcov

# -------------------------------------------
# 1. Load Data
# -------------------------------------------
dt <- fread("comment_takeovers_1975_1991.csv")   # each row = deal

# -------------------------------------------
# 2. Variable Construction
# -------------------------------------------
# Law dummies
dt[, Post_ITSA  := announcement_date >= "1984-10-23" & 
                        announcement_date <= "1988-04-30"]
dt[, Post_ITSFEA:= announcement_date >= "1988-11-19"]

# High-Leak classification (pre-computed list)
hl <- fread("high_leak_sic.csv")  # cols: sic2, high_leak (0/1)
dt <- merge(dt, hl, by = "sic2", all.x = TRUE)
dt[is.na(high_leak), high_leak := 0]

# Exclude wash-out windows
dt <- dt[!(announcement_date %between% c("1984-03-01","1984-10-22")) &
         !(announcement_date %between% c("1988-05-01","1988-11-18"))]

# Instrument
dt[, Z := (Post_ITSA | Post_ITSFEA) * high_leak]

# Controls
dt[, ln_size   := log(target_market_cap)]
dt[, hostile   := as.integer(hostile_bid==1)]
dt[, tender    := as.integer(tender_offer==1)]
dt[, cash_only := as.integer(payment_form=="AllCash")]
dt[, year_fe   := factor(year(announcement_date))]
dt[, ind_fe    := factor(sic2)]

# -------------------------------------------
# 3. 2SLS Estimation
# -------------------------------------------
# Main Specification
iv_formula <- feols(markup ~ 1 | runup ~ Z | ln_size + hostile +
                     tender + cash_only | year_fe + ind_fe, 
                    data = dt, cluster = ~sic2)

summary(iv_formula)

# First-stage F-stat
wald_iv <- wald(iv_formula, keep = "fit_runup", cluster = ~sic2)
print(wald_iv)

# -------------------------------------------
# 4. Robustness Check – Placebo Law (1982)
# -------------------------------------------
dt[, Placebo := (announcement_date >= "1982-01-01" & 
                 announcement_date <= "1982-12-31") * high_leak]

iv_placebo <- feols(markup ~ 1 | runup ~ Placebo | ln_size + hostile +
                      tender + cash_only | year_fe + ind_fe,
                    data = dt, cluster = ~sic2)

summary(iv_placebo)
```

6. EXPECTED RESULTS
----------------------------------------------------------------------
Prior based on bargaining theory:

•  If bidders target a **total** premium driven by expected synergies, any
   exogenous fall in runup should be offset one-for-one by a higher
   markup ⇒ β ≈ –1.  
•  If runups represent pure wealth transfers to target shareholders
   (bidders are “price-takers”), markups won’t adjust ⇒ β ≈ 0.  

Given anecdotal evidence of bidder backlash against inflated prices but
also of contested auctions where bidders get locked in, I expect **partial
substitution**, β ≈ –0.6 (i.e., a $1 increase in runup cuts the markup by
roughly 60 cents).

7. VALIDITY CHECKLIST SELF-ASSESSMENT (IV)
----------------------------------------------------------------------
C1: Strong first stage (F>10) ................. 1  
C2: Exclusion restriction credible ............ 0.8  
C3: Parallel trends visual/pre-trend tests ..... 0.8  
C4: No endogenous sample selection ............ 0.6  
C5: Robustness to alternative specifications ... 1  
Overall ≈ 4.2 / 5  → good but not bullet-proof.

======================================================================
